lessonTitle: Static Failure of Ductile and Brittle Parts

blocks.text: A cast-iron pulley hub that is over-loaded snaps cleanly with no warning, while a steel shaft carrying the same stress bends and gives notice before it fails. The two materials fail in different ways, so the same stress state must be judged by different criteria, and the effect of a notch on each is different too.

blocks.markdown: Static failure means the part has yielded (ductile materials) or fractured (brittle materials) under a load that does not change with time. The practical dividing line is the true strain at fracture: a material with a strain above about 5 per cent is classed as ductile (steels, aluminium), and one below that as brittle (grey cast iron, ceramics, glass). Ductile materials fail by yielding, so the yield strength $S_y$ is the limiting strength, and its yield strength in tension and compression is about the same. Brittle materials have no yield point, fracture suddenly, and are much stronger in compression, $S_{uc}$, than in tension, $S_{ut}$.

blocks.title: Ductile and brittle failure criteria
blocks.text: For ductile materials the **maximum shear stress** (Tresca) criterion predicts yield when $\sigma_1-\sigma_3=S_y$, and the **distortion energy** (von Mises) criterion when $\sigma'=S_y$. For brittle materials the **modified Mohr** criterion uses both the tensile and the compressive strengths, since the material fractures at a different stress in tension than compression. The principal stresses are $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\sigma_3$ and for plane stress $\sigma_A\ge\sigma_B$ denote the two non-zero principal stresses.

blocks.caption: Principal stresses for plane stress and the von Mises stress (MPa)

blocks.markdown: **Stresses at a critical point of a stepped shaft.** The surface of a solid round shaft is a point of plane stress. An axial force $P$ gives a uniform normal stress $4P/(\pi d^2)$, a bending moment $M$ gives $32M/(\pi d^3)$ (largest at the surface, tensile on one side), and a torque $T$ gives a shear stress $16T/(\pi d^3)$. The axial and bending normal stresses simply add algebraically on the tension side, and the shear acts together with them. The critical point is on the surface at the smallest diameter or at a shoulder where the moment is large. The transverse shear force gives zero shear on the extreme fibre and is ignored.

blocks.caption: Combined normal and shear stress at the outer fibre of a solid round shaft (consistent units: N and mm give MPa)

blocks.title: Combined loading of a stepped shaft (ductile)
blocks.prompt: The 40 mm diameter section of a stepped steel shaft ($S_y=380$ MPa, typical) carries an axial tension of 20 kN, a bending moment of 900 N m and a torque of 700 N m. Find the stress at the critical point and the factors of safety by the maximum-shear and von Mises criteria. Ignore stress concentration (ductile, static).

steps.text: Axial, bending and shear stresses with $d^2=1600$ mm$^2$ and $d^3=64000$ mm$^3$.
Total normal stress on the tension side, then principal stresses (with $\sigma_y=0$).
Maximum-shear criterion: $\sigma_1-\sigma_3$ with $\sigma_3=\sigma_B$ the negative principal stress.
Von Mises equivalent stress and factor of safety.

blocks.answer: The critical point has $\sigma_x=159$ MPa and $\tau=56$ MPa; the von Mises factor is 2.04 and the (more conservative) maximum-shear factor is 1.96.

rows: Best fit to test data, standard
Only reliable in the first quadrant
blocks.caption: Failure criteria for static loading

blocks.markdown: **Brittle parts: modified Mohr.** With $\sigma_A\ge\sigma_B$ the factor of safety $n$ of a brittle part is given by three cases. If both principal stresses are tensile ($\sigma_A\ge\sigma_B\ge0$), or if one is compressive of smaller magnitude than the tensile one, then failure is governed by the tensile strength. If the compressive stress exceeds the tensile one in magnitude the failure line slopes between the two strengths. The criterion is generally used with $S_{uc}$ taken as a positive magnitude.

blocks.caption: Modified Mohr factor of safety for a brittle material (tension positive)

blocks.markdown: **Stress concentration in static design.** For a **ductile** part the peak stress at a notch causes only local yielding, which spreads the load and is harmless in static loading, so the nominal stress is used (the main exceptions are low temperature, shock or a material of low ductility). For a **brittle** part there is no yielding to relieve the peak: the full theoretical factor $K_t$ multiplies the nominal stresses, so a notch can cut the load capacity by half or more.

blocks.title: Notch effect on a cast-iron part
blocks.prompt: A grey cast iron part (typical $S_{ut}=215$ MPa, $S_{uc}=750$ MPa) has a nominal plane stress state at a fillet of $\sigma_x=80$ MPa tension and $\tau=50$ MPa with $\sigma_y=0$. Find the factor of safety without and with a stress concentration of $K_t=2.0$ applied to all stresses. Then find the factor of safety for a state with $\sigma_A=60$ MPa and $\sigma_B=-150$ MPa.

steps.text: Compression-dominated state, $|\sigma_B/\sigma_A|=2.5>1$, so use the sloped line.

blocks.answer: Without the notch $n=2.07$; with $K_t=2$ it halves to $n=1.03$, leaving almost no margin. The compression-dominated state has $n=2.51$.

blocks.title: Match the criterion and the notch rule to the material
blocks.text: Ductile: use von Mises (or Tresca for a conservative check) with nominal stress for static loading. Brittle: use modified Mohr with the full $K_t$ applied to the stresses, and use $S_{ut}$ and $S_{uc}$ as magnitudes. In both cases find the combined stress at the critical point first.

points: Ductile parts yield; use von Mises ($\sigma'=S_y/n$) or the more conservative maximum-shear criterion; brittle parts fracture and need $S_{ut}$ and $S_{uc}$ (modified Mohr).
At the outer fibre of a stepped shaft, $\sigma_x=4P/(\pi d^2)+32M/(\pi d^3)$ and $\tau=16T/(\pi d^3)$; find the principal stresses from these.
Modified Mohr: $n=S_{ut}/\sigma_A$ when $|\sigma_B/\sigma_A|\le1$, otherwise use the sloped line with $S_{uc}$.
Stress concentration is neglected for ductile static design, but must be applied in full to brittle parts.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how a brittle material such as grey cast iron fails under static load?

options.text: By sudden fracture without significant yielding, and it is much stronger in compression than in tension
By gradual yielding with large plastic deformation
By fatigue at the first cycle

questions.correctOptionText: By sudden fracture without significant yielding, and it is much stronger in compression than in tension

distractorRationale.a: Correct: brittle materials fracture, and $S_{uc}$ is greater than $S_{ut}$.
distractorRationale.c: Fatigue is a different failure mode and does not describe static loading.
distractorRationale.d: Creep is not the failure mode of static loading at room temperature.

questions.explanation: A brittle material has no plastic range, so cracks run suddenly from flaws that are opened by tension. Because compression closes the flaws, the compressive strength is several times the tensile strength.

questions.stem: For a ductile steel under static load, how is stress concentration at a fillet usually treated?

options.text: It is ignored, because local yielding relieves the peak stress without loss of strength
The full $K_t$ is always applied to the nominal stress
$K_t$ is applied only to the shear stress
The concentration is applied to the yield strength instead

questions.correctOptionText: It is ignored, because local yielding relieves the peak stress without loss of strength

distractorRationale.a: Correct: local yielding redistributes the load, so nominal stresses are used.
distractorRationale.c: There is no special rule for shear only.
distractorRationale.d: Stress concentration is a stress multiplier, not a change in strength.

questions.explanation: In a ductile material the peak stress produces a small yielded zone that strain-hardens and spreads the load, so net strength is hardly affected. A concentration must be applied in fatigue or for brittle materials.

questions.stem: A ductile part is analysed using both the maximum-shear (Tresca) criterion and the von Mises criterion for the same stress state. What is the usual relationship between the factors of safety?

options.text: The Tresca factor is the same or smaller, so it is the more conservative
The Tresca factor is always larger
Von Mises always gives the smaller factor

questions.correctOptionText: The Tresca factor is the same or smaller, so it is the more conservative

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the Tresca hexagon lies inside or on the von Mises ellipse.
distractorRationale.c: They agree only for certain stress states, such as uniaxial tension.
distractorRationale.d: Von Mises predicts yield later than Tresca.

questions.explanation: The Tresca yield locus is inscribed in the von Mises ellipse, so it predicts yielding no later than von Mises. The two coincide in uniaxial tension and differ by up to 15 per cent in pure shear.

questions.stem: A grey cast iron part ($S_{ut}=215$ MPa, $S_{uc}=750$ MPa) has principal stresses $\sigma_A=100$ MPa and $\sigma_B=-40$ MPa. What is the modified-Mohr factor of safety?

distractorRationale.b: 7.5 uses the compressive strength in place of the tensile strength (750/100).
distractorRationale.c: 1.54 uses Sut/(sigma_A - sigma_B), a maximum-shear style difference that does not apply to brittle fracture.
distractorRationale.d: 5.4 uses Suc/(sigma_A - sigma_B), which is also not part of the criterion.

questions.explanation: Since the compressive principal stress is smaller in magnitude than the tensile one, the tensile strength governs and $n=S_{ut}/\sigma_A=215/100=2.15$. The sloped line with $S_{uc}$ only matters when $|\sigma_B|>\sigma_A$.

questions.stem: Which stress components act at the critical outer-fibre point of a shaft that carries axial tension, bending and torque?

options.text: A normal stress from the axial force plus the bending stress, and a shear stress from the torque
Only the shear stress from the torque
The transverse shear stress is the largest contribution

questions.correctOptionText: A normal stress from the axial force plus the bending stress, and a shear stress from the torque

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the normal stresses add and the torque gives shear.
distractorRationale.b: The axial force and the torque also contribute.
distractorRationale.c: The normal stresses are also present.
distractorRationale.d: Transverse shear is zero at the extreme fibre.

questions.explanation: On the tension side the axial and bending normal stresses add, and the torque produces a shear stress there. The transverse shear force is zero at the outer fibre, so it is neglected in the critical-point analysis.

questions.stem: A solid shaft of diameter 35 mm carries an axial tension of 30 kN and a bending moment of 500 N m. Find the largest tensile normal stress at the surface in MPa.
questions.explanation: The axial stress is $4\times30000/(\pi\times35^2)=31.2$ MPa and the bending stress is $32\times500000/(\pi\times35^3)=118.8$ MPa. On the tension side they add, giving $150.0$ MPa.

questions.stem: At the critical point of a steel part ($S_y=350$ MPa) the stress state is $\sigma_x=100$ MPa, $\sigma_y=0$ and $\tau_{xy}=60$ MPa. Use the maximum-shear (Tresca) criterion to find the factor of safety (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: The maximum in-plane shear stress is $\tau_{max}=\sqrt{(100/2)^2+60^2}=78.1$ MPa, so $\sigma_1-\sigma_2=2\tau_{max}=156.2$ MPa. Then $n=S_y/(\sigma_1-\sigma_2)=350/156.2=2.24$.

questions.stem: A grey cast iron part ($S_{ut}=215$ MPa, $S_{uc}=750$ MPa) has a nominal stress state at a fillet of $\sigma_x=70$ MPa and $\tau_{xy}=40$ MPa ($\sigma_y=0$). The fillet has a stress concentration factor $K_t=2.4$ that must be applied to all stresses. Find the modified-Mohr factor of safety (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: With $K_t=2.4$, $\sigma_x=168$ MPa and $\tau=96$ MPa. The principal stresses are $\sigma_A=84+\sqrt{84^2+96^2}=211.6$ MPa and $\sigma_B=-43.6$ MPa, with $|\sigma_B/\sigma_A|=0.21<1$. So $n=215/211.6=1.02$, essentially no margin.

questions.stem: For a stepped shaft carrying an axial force, a bending moment and a torque, describe how you would find the factor of safety at the critical point for a ductile steel, stating the equations and the criterion used.
markingGuide: Locate the critical section and point: surface at the smallest diameter or shoulder where moment is large, on the tension side of the bending.
Axial stress $4P/(\pi d^2)$, bending stress $32M/(\pi d^3)$ (add on the tension side), shear stress $16T/(\pi d^3)$; transverse shear is zero at the outer fibre.
Von Mises $\sigma'=\sqrt{\sigma_x^2+3\tau^2}$ and $n=S_y/\sigma'$ (Tresca: $n=S_y/(\sigma_A-\sigma_B)$ as a conservative check).
Stress concentration ignored for ductile static loading; compare $n$ with the design factor.
questions.explanation: The method reduces a combined load to one equivalent stress that can be compared with the yield strength. The critical point is identified from the stress distribution, not from the load alone.

questions.stem: Explain why stress concentration is generally ignored in the static design of ductile parts but must be included for brittle parts, and describe how the modified Mohr criterion is used for a brittle part in a plane stress state.
markingGuide: Ductile: local yielding at the notch redistributes the load, the yielded zone is small, and net strength is hardly reduced; strain hardening gives additional margin.
Brittle: no yielding, so the peak stress $K_t\sigma_{nom}$ is the stress that initiates fracture; the nominal stresses must be multiplied by $K_t$.
Exceptions: ductile parts at low temperature, under shock, or with very low ductility behave more like brittle ones.
Modified Mohr: compute principal stresses $\sigma_A\ge\sigma_B$ (with $K_t$ applied); if $\sigma_A\ge0$ and $|\sigma_B/\sigma_A|\le1$, $n=S_{ut}/\sigma_A$.

If $\sigma_B<0$ and $|\sigma_B|>\sigma_A$, use $1/n=\frac{S_{uc}-S_{ut}}{S_{uc}S_{ut}}\sigma_A-\sigma_B/S_{uc}$, with $S_{uc}$ as a positive magnitude, which accounts for the much greater compressive strength.
questions.explanation: Notches are harmless to ductile material in static loading because they only cause local yielding. In brittle materials they directly initiate the fracture.
